title: The General Who Won Five Campaigns With Nothing — Then Got Sacked By Churchill
fullText: Five campaigns won with almost nothing. Nine countries defended at the same time. Over 130,000 enemy soldiers captured in a single offensive. And then [music] a telegram arrives at breakfast telling you that you have been fired. Archerald Waveville [music] was the British general who held the entire Middle East and East Africa together during the darkest [music] stretch of the Second World War. fighting across two continents with a fraction of the troops he needed, [music] pulling off victories that should not have been possible. But the one man he could never win over was his own prime minister. And that failure cost him everything. To understand how the most overworked [music] commander in British history ended up pushed aside, you have to go back to where it started. Archable Persal Wavel was born on the 5th of May 1883 in Colchester, England. His father was a major general, so the army was in his blood before he could walk. He won a scholarship to Winchester College, one of the most academically demanding schools in the country, and from there went straight to the Royal Military College at Sandhurst. He graduated and was commissioned into the Black Watch regiment in 1901, and within months he was fighting in the Second Bore War [music] in South Africa. He was barely 18. But Wville was not just a soldier. He was something rare in the British army of that era. An intellectual who read voraciously, memorized [music] poetry by the hundreds of pages and later compiled an entire anthology of his favorite poems called Other Men's Flowers. He spoke multiple languages. He contributed articles to the Encyclopedia Britannica. He named his training exercises after Greek myths. And yet for all that bookishness, he was a frontline officer who insisted on seeing the terrain and the men himself, not commanding from a shadow behind the lines. When the First World War broke [music] out in 1914, Waveville went straight to France. He fought in the trenches, [music] got wounded, earned the Military Cross for bravery. And then in June 1915, during the second battle [music] of Eprey, a shell splinter tore through his face. He lost his left [music] eye. He was 32 years old, newly married to Eujenei Marie Quirk, and now he had to decide whether the army was still his future. It was not even a question. After a short recovery, [music] he was back in the war. He ended up serving under General Edmund Alenby in Palestine, riding alongside Te Lawrence during [music] the campaign against the Ottoman Turks, entering Jerusalem, and advancing all the way to Damascus. He admired Alani so much that he eventually wrote three books about him [music] and modeled his entire approach to command on Alen's aggressive flexible style. Between the wars, Waveville climbed the ranks and built a reputation as the best trainer of troops in the British army. He commanded the sixth infantry brigade, then the second division, and by 1937, he was running British forces [music] in Palestine and Trans Jordan during a period of serious political unrest. He believed in mobility, deception, [music] and unorthodox thinking. He was the first commander to conduct a long tactical advance of troops using road transport, a fleet of buses, no less. He named training exercises [music] after Greek myths, because he thought soldiers who understood stories fought with more imagination. He once told [music] subordinates that an officer should never under any circumstances think a cause [music] or a battle lost. But Waveville had a weakness that no battlefield victory could fix. He was quiet. Not the thoughtful kind of quiet that people mistake for depth. The kind of quiet that made powerful people uncomfortable. He could write with clarity and precision. He could plan campaigns that spanned continents. But in a room with someone who expected conversation, he froze. He struggled to explain himself out loud and he had no patience for politicians who needed to be charmed or flattered. Historian Carlo Dest called [music] him a bright aggressive commander of the sort that was in desperately short supply in the Morabund British Army of 1940 [music] and 1941. But brightness and aggression on the battlefield [music] meant nothing if you could not sell yourself across a dinner table. That flaw would not matter as long as Waveville answered to other soldiers. But in July 1939, [music] he was handed the most sprawling military command in British history. And his new boss was a man who lived and breathed [music] words, Winston Churchill. Waveville's Middle East command covered Egypt, Sudan, Palestine, Trans Jordan, Cyprus, Aiden, Iraq, British Somaliand, and the Persian Gulf. nine countries, two continents, an [music] area of 1,700 mi by 2,000 mi, and he was given five staff officers to manage [music] all of it. The job was to protect the Suez Canal and British oil interests and to prepare for a war that everyone knew was coming. When it came, it came from all directions at once. [music] Italy entered the war on the 10th of June, 1940, and the numbers were staggering. Marshall Rodulfo Gratzani had roughly 200,000 Italian and Libyan troops stationed across the border in Libya. In Italian East Africa, meaning Eratraa, Ethiopia, and Italian [music] Somaliand, the Duke of Aosta commanded another 250,000. We had about 40,000 troops total. He was outnumbered more than 10 to one. In September 1940, the Italians crossed the Egyptian border with a massive force and pushed 60 mi into Egypt before stopping at a cluster of fortified camps [music] around the town of Sidi Barani. Gratzani dug in and waited for supplies. Wavvel [music] did not wait. He had been planning a counterattack, a large-scale raid [music] designed to hit the Italians where they were weakest. He called it Operation Compass and he gave the job to Lieutenant General Richard O'Conor, a sharp and aggressive officer who commanded the Western Desert Force. The numbers [music] tell you everything about what happened next. Okconor had 36,000 [music] men, two divisions, both below strength. Facing them were 150,000 Italians in fortified positions with more artillery and more vehicles. Compass was supposed to be a [music] 5-day raid. It turned into a two-month route. On the 9th of December 1940, Okconor's men hit the [music] Italian camp at Nibbea at dawn. Artillery, armor, and infantry [music] struck together in a textbook combined arms assault. The Italians [music] were stunned. Their M1139 tanks could not penetrate the armor of the British Matilda tanks and the defenders crumbled so fast that whole [music] divisions surrendered in hours. Within 2 days, the British had swept through the chain [music] of camps around Sidi Barani and captured nearly 40,000 prisoners. Okconor did not stop. He chased the retreating Italians across the Libyan border, took the port of Bardia on the 3rd of January with Australian reinforcements, and then pushed on to Tbrook, which fell on the 22nd of January, [music] 1941. But the most astonishing moment came at the very end. In early February, with the remnants of the Italian 10th Army [music] retreating west along the coastal road toward Tripoli, Okconor sent an armored column on a wild shortcut straight across the desert to cut them off at a place called Bedafom. 3,000 men with 86 tanks raced 150 mi through the open desert, arrived ahead [music] of the Italians, and blocked the road. When the Italian columns slammed into the roadblock, it was over. Okconor sent a message to Wavel that said simply, "Fox killed in the [music] open." In two months, Wavel and Okconor had advanced over [music] 500 miles, captured 133,000 prisoners, taken 420 tanks, and [music] 845 guns, and destroyed an entire army. The cost was 500 British [music] and Commonwealth soldiers killed. To put that in perspective, for every British soldier who died, [music] they captured more than 260 enemy troops, that is not just a victory. That is one of the most lopsided results in the history of modern warfare. And the timing mattered as much as the numbers. This was the winter of 1940 to 1941. Britain was fighting alone. France had fallen. The British Expeditionary Force had been thrown out of Europe at Dunkirk 6 months earlier. The Blitz was hammering London every night. America was still neutral. The entire war felt like a slow march toward defeat. And then [music] out of the Egyptian desert came this impossible victory. The news that a tiny British force had routed an Italian army five times its size and chased it across Libya sent a jolt through [music] the entire Allied world. in Washington. It helped push the lend lease bill through the American [music] Congress on the 8th of February 1941, one day after better. Waveville's victory [music] did not just change the map of North Africa. It changed the mood of the war. And Waveville was just getting started because at the exact same time he was planning Compass, he was already preparing an invasion of Italian East Africa. The situation down there was just as lopsided. [music] The Duke of Aosta had nearly 300,000 Italian and colonial troops dug into Eritraa, Ethiopia, [music] and Italian Somaliand. Wavel had maybe 70,000 Commonwealth soldiers from across the empire, Indian divisions, South African units, Sudanese and Nigerian troops, plus irregular Ethiopian forces loyal to the exiled Emperor Hayel Salassi. He launched a three-pronged assault in January [music] 1941. One force drove from Sudan into Eratria. Another pushed north from Kenya into Italian Somali land. And a third crossed from Aiden to retake British Somali land. The Eratrian advance hit the hardest resistance. At the mountain fortress of Kerin, two Indian divisions fought a brutal six-week battle against Italian defenders dug into cliff faces [music] and ridge lines. Kerin finally fell on the 27th of March and the port of Masawa followed [music] on the 8th of April. Meanwhile, the advance from Kenya was covering ground so fast that the [music] campaign was outpacing anyone's estimates. Lieutenant General Alan Cunningham's forces swept through Italian Somaliand and pushed deep [music] into Ethiopia. By April, British troops entered Addis Ababa and on the 5th of May, Emperor Halele Salassi returned to his capital [music] in triumph. In 5 months, Waveville had conquered an empire. An area the size of Western Europe [music] had been taken from Italy with a force that was outnumbered 4 to1. It was one of the fastest and most complete [music] military victories of the entire war. And today, most people have never even heard of it. But here is where the story turns. Because while pulling off these victories with one hand, Churchill was tying the other one behind his back. In February 1941, right in the middle of the Compass advance, Churchill ordered Waveville to divert nearly 60,000 of his best troops to Greece. The Greek government was struggling against an Italian invasion, and Churchill saw a political opportunity to open a new front in the Balkans. Wavvel disagreed. He knew the Greek expedition [music] was likely to fail, and he knew it would gut his forces in North Africa just when they had the Italians [music] on the run. Okconor himself believed he could have pushed all the way to Tripoli and thrown [music] the Italians out of Libya completely, but Churchill insisted and Wavel obeyed. The Greek campaign [music] was a disaster. The Germans intervened with overwhelming air and ground power and the British and Commonwealth force was thrown out in weeks, suffering heavy casualties and losing [music] enormous amounts of equipment. The island of Cree fell soon after. Wavel lost his best units, his best equipment, and the momentum of Operation Compass, all for nothing. And the consequences were immediate because in February 1941, the same month, Wavel was forced to strip his desert army and send his [music] best divisions to the Balkans. A new German general arrived in the port of Tripoli with a small but ferocious armored force called the Africa Corpse. His name was Irwin Raml. He had orders from Berlin to hold the line and stabilize the Italian [music] position. He ignored them completely. Within days of landing, RML attacked and RML was everything. Wavevel was not in one specific way. RML was a [music] showman. He was reckless, bold, theatrical, and he did not ask permission before he moved. He sized up the situation in Libya, saw that the British forces [music] had been gutted by the Greek deployment, and launched a counteroffensive that caught everyone [music] off guard. Within weeks, Raml had pushed Wavel's weakened forces all the way back across Libya, recapturing almost everything that Compass had won. Benghazi fell. [music] The coastal road was lost. Only the port of Tbrook held out, besieged [music] and surrounded. Okconor himself was captured during the chaotic retreat, picked up by a German [music] patrol while driving at night. The brilliant general who had sent that famous message, Fox killed in the open, was now a prisoner of war. The desert fox had arrived, and [music] Wavel suddenly found himself fighting on the defensive with forces that were already stretched past the [music] point of survival. The victories of December and January felt like ancient history. And the worst part was that Waveville had warned [music] this would happen. He had told Churchill that stripping his army for Greece would leave North Africa dangerously exposed. He had been right. But being right and being heard are two very different things. And still the fires kept multiplying. In April 1941, a pro-axis politician named Rashid Ali staged a coup in Baghdad with [music] German backing and besieged the Royal Air Force base at Habania just outside the city. Iraq was critical. Its oil fields fed the entire British war machine in the Middle East. If Rashid Ali held power, the oil stopped flowing and the whole theater collapsed. Wavevel already managing the North African front against Raml. the [music] East Africa campaign and the aftermath of the Greek catastrophe was ordered to deal with it. He hesitated at first because he genuinely did not have forces to spare. Churchill was furious at the delay. Wavel eventually assembled a relief column that broke through to Habania and by the end of May, Rashid Ali had fled to Berlin. Then in June, Wavelunched [music] yet another operation. This time a full invasion of Vishy French, Syria and Lebanon. French forces loyal to the collaborationist [music] Vichi government had been allowing German aircraft to refuel on their airfields and Churchill demanded that the threat be removed before the Germans could turn Syria [music] into a staging ground. Think about what all of that means. Between June 1940 and June 1941, a single commander working from a headquarters in Cairo with a handful of staff officers fought simultaneous campaigns across Libya, Egypt, Sudan, Eratraa, Ethiopia, Italian Somaliand, British Somaliand, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Greece, and [music] Cree. He crushed two separate Italian armies against absurd odds. He conquered an enemy empire the size of Western Europe. He put down a pro-Nazi revolt in Iraq. He invaded and seized French- held territory in the Levant. He did all of it with forces that were always too small against enemies that always outnumbered him while being forced to send his best troops to a doomed Balkan campaign [music] that he had warned against from the beginning. In those 12 months, he was the only British theater commander in the entire world who was actively fighting the axis on land. The only one. But Churchill did not see it that way. The problem between Waveville and Churchill was personal before it was professional. Churchill was the most verbal leader in the English-speaking [music] world. A man who thought in speeches and demanded constant communication, reports, explanations, arguments. Wavel was the opposite. Historian Carelli Barnett described [music] him as absolutely tongue-tied around Churchill. Wavel could not smoo. He could not perform. When Churchill visited Cairo, Wavel [music] sat in silence while Churchill filled the room. Churchill interpreted that silence [music] as passivity, as a lack of fighting spirit. The irony was vicious. The general who was actually fighting [music] more campaigns simultaneously than almost any commander in history [music] was being judged by a man who confused talking about war with waging it. Churchill started losing faith in WAVL long before Operation Battleax. The constant stream of urgent telegrams from London demanding faster offensives, more aggressive action, and bigger results wore on both men. Wavel resented being second-guessed by a politician hundreds of miles from the front. Churchill [music] resented what he saw as a commander who kept making excuses instead of attacking. The chief of the Imperial [music] General Staff, John Dill, privately warned Waveville that the prime minister was losing confidence in him. Dill told [music] him bluntly that if Churchill no longer trusted him, he should be replaced. Then came the breaking point. Churchill had personally organized a risky convoy cenamed Tiger to rush nearly 300 [music] tanks through the Mediterranean to reinforce Waveville. Churchill called them his Tiger [music] Cubs and expected them to be sent straight into action. Wavel signaled back that the tanks had arrived with mechanical faults, that crews [music] needed time to train on them, and that an immediate attack was premature. Churchill was furious. Under intense pressure, Wavelunched Operation [music] Battle Axe on the 15th of June, 1941. The goal was to push Raml back from the Egyptian border [music] and lift the siege of Tbrook. It was the first time British forces engaged the Germans in a major defensive position in the desert. And it went badly from [music] the start. RML had studied the earlier British attacks and lined Hellfire Pass with anti-tank guns that shredded the Matilda tanks. The British lost over half their tanks [music] on the first day. On the second day, results were mixed. On the third day, the British narrowly avoided encirclement and [music] had to withdraw. The operation was over in 3 days. British casualties [music] were about 970 men, killed, wounded, and missing. It was a defeat, but it was not a catastrophe. The army survived [music] intact. RML's own forces were exhausted and badly stretched on their supply lines. The Germans had only 25 tanks [music] written off compared to the British losses of 87 total. But RML's fuel situation was desperate and he could not exploit the victory. A more patient assessment might have recognized that Waveville was being asked to do the impossible. He was attacking with mechanically unreliable equipment against a general who had spent weeks preparing defensive positions using tanks that had arrived with known faults with crews who barely had time to learn how to drive them after losing his best units to a Greek campaign he never wanted. But Churchill was not [music] patient. He had already made up his mind weeks before Battleax even launched. The operation was less a genuine test than it was the last excuse Churchill [music] needed to do what he had been wanting to do for months. On the morning of June 21st, 1941, Waveville's chief of staff, Lieutenant General Sir Arthur Smith, walked into the general's house in Cairo before breakfast carrying [music] a telegram. It informed Waveville that he was being relieved of his command and swapped with General Claude Orinch, the commander and chief of India. Wavel read the message, set it down, and said, [music] "The prime minister is quite right. There ought to be a fresh eye and a fresh mind [music] on the problems here. I have been out here since 1939." Churchill later wrote that [music] Waveville received the decision with poise and dignity. Years afterward, Churchill reflected on the moment and said something surprisingly [music] honest. He said, "It was a terrible thing to have to do. He took it [music] like a gentleman. It is difficult to remove a bad general at the height of a campaign. It is atrocious to remove a good general. And that word atrocious tells you everything about how Churchill felt about what he had done. He knew Wavel was good. He just could not work with him. Wavevel went to India and took Alkinlech's old job as commanderin-chief. He was appalled at what he found. The defenses were in shambles. There were only obsolete fighter planes, no modern tanks or armored cars, and barely 30 anti-aircraft guns in the entire country. And when Japan attacked in December 1941, Waveville was handed yet another impossible task. He was given command of Abdicom, the combined American, British, Dutch, and Australian command trying to stop the Japanese advance through Southeast Asia. It was a paper coalition with no real combined structure, no shared doctrine, and nowhere near enough troops. The Japanese blew through the defenses of Malaya, Singapore, and the Dutch East Indies with a speed that shocked [music] everyone. During the chaos, Waveville himself fell over a barbed wire seaw wall in Singapore and was rushed to hospital for 4 days, leaving the command structure temporarily [music] leaderless. Abdicom was disbanded on the 23rd of February 1942, less than a month after it was created. The fall of Singapore was the largest British military surrender in history. And although we was not the direct cause, his name was attached to it. He stayed on [music] as commander in Chief India, reorganizing the defenses and laying [music] groundwork that later commanders would build on. Then in October 1943, Churchill offered him the position of viceroy of India. It was an elegant way to move him out of military command entirely. Wavel accepted. As viceroy, he faced a crisis that had nothing to do with tanks and guns. The Bengal famine of 1943 had already killed [music] an estimated 1 and a half to 3 million people by the time Wavevel took office. He ordered the army to distribute relief supplies to rural populations and fought to get shipments of grain to the starving provinces. He knew that 6 million tons of wheat sat in British storage vessels floating nearby reserved for military emergencies and he [music] lobbied hard to get them released. He did what he could but the political situation in India was beyond [music] any one man's control. Gandhi was leading the quit India movement from prison. Jina was demanding [music] a separate Muslim state called Pakistan. Subaz Chandra Bose had allied himself with the Japanese and was pushing toward India's eastern border with an army of Indian defectors. Waveville convened the [music] similar conference in 1945 to bring the factions together, pushed plans for an orderly transition to self-government and tried to prevent the communal violence that he knew partition would bring. He was against partition and warned it would lead to bloodshed. He was right about that too. In the end, Prime Minister Clement Atley decided Waveville was too cautious and too [music] old-fashioned for the speed London wanted and replaced him with Lord Mountbatton in February 1947. For the second time in his career, a politician chose a different personality for the job, not a more capable one. Once [music] again, Waveville was pushed aside because a politician wanted a different personality in the job, not necessarily a more capable one. [music] He returned to England, accepted anom, and was granted the additional title of Vic Counter, named after the brutal battle in Eratria that his forces had won. He became constable of the Tower of London and president of the Royal Society of Literature, the Kipling Society, the Browning [music] Society, and several poetry organizations. The soldier, who had memorized [music] entire anthologies by heart, found his way back to the books that had sustained him through a [music] lifetime of impossible situations. On the 24th of May 1950, Archerald Wavevel [music] died in London following a relapse after surgery. He was 67 years old. His funeral was held at Westminster Abbey with full military honors and he was buried in the closter at Winchester College where he had been a school boy more than half a century earlier. The man RML himself once praised as the only British desert general who showed a touch of genius was laid to rest without the [music] fame that later commanders enjoyed. Montgomery got Elmagne and all the glory that came with it. Slim got Burma. [music] Alexander got Italy, but Montgomery fought with overwhelming superiority in numbers, equipment, [music] and air power. He fought with American supplies pouring in and an enemy whose fuel lines were collapsing. Wavel fought with nothing. [music] He fought outnumbered 5 to one and won. He fought across nine [music] countries and two continents at the same time and won nearly all of them. He managed simultaneous [music] campaigns that no modern staff college would ever ask a [music] single officer to handle. Campaigns that spanned from the Libyan desert to the mountains of Eratraa to the streets of Baghdad to the cedars of Lebanon. And he won most of them while [music] being told by his own prime minister that he was not aggressive enough. General Orinch, the man who replaced Waveville, lasted barely a year before Churchill sacked him too for the same reasons. It turned out that the problem was not always the general. What Wavel could not do [music] was talk about his victories in a way that made Churchill feel like a partner instead of a spectator. And in a war where political relationships mattered as much as battlefield results, that silence was a fatal weakness. Sometimes the most capable person in the room is the quietest one. And sometimes that is [music] exactly why they get replaced. If this story surprised you, hit subscribe and leave a comment telling us which forgotten commander deserves a video next. And if you are already subscribed, tap the like button so more people can [music] find these stories.
fullTextVi: Năm chiến dịch hầu như không thắng được gì. Chín nước đồng thời phòng thủ. Hơn 130.000 quân địch bị bắt chỉ trong một cuộc tấn công. Và sau đó [âm nhạc] một bức điện đến vào bữa sáng thông báo với bạn rằng bạn đã bị sa thải. Archerald Waveville [âm nhạc] là vị tướng người Anh nắm giữ toàn bộ Trung Đông và Đông Phi cùng nhau trải qua [âm nhạc] đen tối nhất trong Thế chiến thứ hai. chiến đấu xuyên suốt hai lục địa với một phần quân số mà anh ta cần, [âm nhạc] kéo giành được những chiến thắng lẽ ra không thể có được. Nhưng người duy nhất mà ông không bao giờ có thể thuyết phục được chính là thủ tướng của chính ông. Và thất bại đó đã khiến anh phải trả giá bằng mọi thứ. Để hiểu người chỉ huy [âm nhạc] làm việc quá sức nhất trong lịch sử nước Anh cuối cùng lại bị đẩy sang một bên, bạn phải quay lại nơi nó bắt đầu. Archable Persal Wavel sinh ngày 5 tháng 5 năm 1883 tại Colchester, Anh. Cha ông là thiếu tướng nên quân đội đã có trong máu ông trước đây anh ấy có thể đi bộ. Anh đã giành được học bổng vào Winchester College, một trong những trường có yêu cầu học tập cao nhất trong nước, và từ đó vào thẳng Trường Cao đẳng Quân sự Hoàng gia tại Sandhurst. Ông tốt nghiệp và được đưa vào trung đoàn Black Watch vào năm 1901, và trong phạm vi tháng anh ấy chiến đấu trong [âm nhạc] Chiến tranh Bore lần thứ hai ở Nam Phi. Anh ấy chỉ mới 18 tuổi. Nhưng Wville không chỉ là một người lính. Anh ta là một điều hiếm thấy trong quân đội Anh thời đó. Một trí thức đọc ngấu nghiến, thuộc lòng thơ hàng trăm trang và sau đó đã biên soạn toàn bộ tuyển tập những bài thơ yêu thích của ông có tên Những bông hoa của đàn ông khác. Anh ấy nói được nhiều thứ tiếng. Ông đã đóng góp nhiều bài viết cho Bách khoa toàn thư Britannica. Ông đặt tên các bài tập huấn luyện của mình theo thần thoại Hy Lạp. Tuy nhiên, với tất cả sự ham mê sách vở đó, anh ta vẫn là một sĩ quan tiền tuyến luôn kiên quyết nhìn thấy địa hình và bản thân những người đàn ông, không chỉ huy từ một cái bóng phía sau dòng. Khi Chiến tranh thế giới thứ nhất nổ ra [âm nhạc] vào năm 1914, Waveville đã đi thẳng vào Pháp. Anh ấy chiến đấu trong chiến hào, [âm nhạc] bị thương, được tặng Huân chương Quân công vì lòng dũng cảm. Và sau đó vào tháng 6 năm 1915, trong trận chiến [âm nhạc] thứ hai ở Eprey, một quả đạn pháo mảnh vụn xé nát mặt anh. Anh ấy bị mất mắt [âm nhạc] trái. Anh ấy 32 tuổi, mới kết hôn với Eujenei Marie Quirk, và bây giờ anh ấy phải quyết định xem quân đội có còn là tương lai của mình hay không. Đó thậm chí không phải là một câu hỏi. Sau một thời gian ngắn hồi phục, [âm nhạc] anh ấy đã trở lại chiến tranh. Cuối cùng ông phục vụ dưới quyền Tướng Edmund Alenby ở Palestine, sát cánh cùng Te Lawrence trong [âm nhạc] chiến dịch chống lại người Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ Ottoman, tiến vào Jerusalem và tiến quân khắp đường tới Damacus. Anh ấy ngưỡng mộ Alani đến mức cuối cùng đã viết ba cuốn sách về anh ấy [âm nhạc] và mô hình hóa toàn bộ cách tiếp cận chỉ huy của mình theo phong cách linh hoạt năng nổ của Alen. Giữa các cuộc chiến, Waveville leo lên cấp bậc và tạo dựng được danh tiếng là người giỏi nhất huấn luyện quân đội trong quân đội Anh.
